19. **The living map.** (added 29 October 2026) Haakon: "In time I want environmental effects, seasons reflected on the map. Characters, armies, fighting shown, etc. Everything you can think of, which makes it a better game for a player or viewer. But I don't believe the time for these effects are quiet yet." With every feature built, the map's look becomes a blend of Imperator: Rome's map and a museum map of the Bronze Age world ("The map in true geography, and its look in time" under Interface): the environment and the seasons on the map, characters, armies and battles as they travel and fight, every unit and figure drawn after the period's own relics in its culture's idiom, a map that remembers the war, life drawn from the simulation, every level of what is built (roads by quality, harbours and docks, walls, water works, granaries, mines), a seasonal year, each realm's own map drawn by its scribes, omens in the margin and small scenes at big moments, and whatever else makes the game better to play or to watch, each measured on a throttled phone. Presentation only, with no change to rules, numbers or balance, so it may run beside item 18. **Stop for review.** Then **19+, answers to 19's review** (30 October 2026; Haakon: "Yes to all"): each realm's own map pressed in clay for every court that writes cuneiform, as the period's clay maps were, and on papyrus for Egypt; a sacked city stays in ruins until its people come back, and they come back by the rule that already moves them ("Feeding a province draws its people": settled people move towards more room, measured in food, and the loose drift towards richer land), so the ruins fade as its people return and its walls are rebuilt with item 15's works, with no rule for rebuilding (Haakon: "no special rules for cities recovering, people will migrate back at the harvest potential difference there becomes bigger than neighboring cities"); and Egypt's view gets hieratic notes as decoration only, the map's own text staying in the reader's language. Presentation only. Then **19++, the visual pass** (30 October 2026; Haakon: "I also think amarna letters needs another visual pass. With the instructions to make it as visually impressive as it possibly can, without tanking the performance."): every screen, not only the map, made as impressive as it can be: the map at every zoom, the province card, the seat view, the letters and their tablets, the council, the chronicle, replay and god view, menus and the first screen, in light and dark, on phone and desktop. One look throughout, in the style the living map set (Imperator: Rome's map and a museum map of the Bronze Age, each culture drawn in its own idiom after the period's relics), with type, colour, texture, light, motion and the small touches that make a game feel crafted, never clutter that hides what a king needs to read. The bound is that it stays playable on a phone (Haakon: "Well, it can get slower, but must be playable on a phone. That's the criteria."): measured as item 19 measures it, on a throttled phone in the busiest scene of each screen, smooth enough to read and play and to watch at top speed without falling behind, with reduced motion respected; it may cost more than now where it buys something worth seeing. The pass starts by finding every graphical glitch and inconsistency on every screen (Haakon: "There are also many graphical glitches and Inconsistencies in the game right now."): things drawn wrong, out of place, overlapping or flickering, and the same thing drawn or named differently in two places; each is listed in the PR with its picture and fixed. The PR shows every screen before and after at 390 px and desktop 2x, light and dark, with the performance numbers before and after. Presentation only, so it may run beside item 18.
